deck: 30 Thinking in Java::11 Holding Your Objects

cards.front: Why do containers exist when arrays already hold objects?
cards.back: Containers resize themselves; arrays have a fixed length chosen at creation
cards.extra: You rarely know how many objects a program will need. The book's point: an array is the most efficient container, but only when the count is known and fixed.

cards.front: What are the four basic container types in java.util?
cards.extra: List keeps order and allows duplicates; Set forbids duplicates; Queue is for processing order; Map associates keys with values. Each answers a different question.

cards.back: At most one element for each value
cards.extra: Adding a duplicate leaves the set unchanged. Uniqueness is decided by equals/hashCode, which is why those methods matter so much for elements.

cards.back: An associative array: it stores key → value pairs
cards.extra: You look values up by key rather than by index. Keys are unique, values may repeat, and iteration order depends on the implementation.

cards.back: Walking a container element by element without knowing its structure
cards.extra: hasNext(), next(), and remove() are the whole contract. It is the Iterator design pattern, which is why it works the same across containers.
Iterator can only go forward and remove. ListIterator is List-specific because indexed order is what makes backwards movement meaningful.

cards.front: Why did generics matter for containers?
cards.back: They make the compiler reject the wrong type at compile time
cards.extra: Before Java SE5 a container held Object, so an Apple could be stored in a list of Oranges and only fail when you cast on retrieval.

cards.front: ArrayList versus LinkedList: what is the real trade-off?
cards.back: Array-backed random access versus node-based cheap insertion
cards.extra: ArrayList gives O(1) get by index and is usually faster in practice; LinkedList wins only for frequent insert/remove in the middle and for Deque behaviour.

cards.front: What behaviour does a Queue add to a collection?
cards.back: Elements are removed in a defined order — typically first-in, first-out
cards.extra: PriorityQueue instead orders by comparison, so the "next" element is the smallest by your comparator, not the oldest.
